<!-- data-checksum: f354a6da47f62ead35825a3d2b8ef6d9 -->

Two things measured on the same patients: femoral torsion on CT and on the modified Budin view, PROM improvement and satisfaction, ASA class and hypertension. The tests on this page don't compare groups. They put **one number on how strongly the two go together**, with a 95% CI. If you want to **predict** one from the other, use regression ([page 11](11-predict-from-one.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 How every section on this page works
Each section answers one question about one of the practice's datasets (hip imaging for Pearson, the joint replacement cohort otherwise). Its first code block loads the packages and the data, so you can jump straight to the section you need. Run that section's blocks in order, top to bottom.

To keep the code short, the joint replacement examples use every case, including both cases of patients who had both sides operated on (80 patients in the whole cohort; [page 2](../foundations/02-demographics.qmd#setup) counts them). In a real study, decide how to handle them ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#paired)) and say what you did.
:::

## Pearson correlation {#pearson}

**The question:** How closely does femoral torsion on the modified Budin view track torsion on CT?

### When to use it

- Two **measurements** on the same patients, and you want one number for how closely they move together along a **straight line**.
- Both are roughly normal, without extreme outliers, and the scatter plot looks like a cloud stretched along a line.
- If either is [skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term} or ordinal, has outliers, or the points follow a curve → [Spearman correlation](#spearman).
- If you want to predict one from the other, or adjust for other variables → [linear regression](11-predict-from-one.qmd#linear-regression).

### What the test really does

Pearson's r measures how closely the points follow a straight line.

1. For each patient, work out how far each of the two measurements is from its own [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term}, counted in [standard deviations](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term}. A hip that lies 1 standard deviation above the mean on CT scores +1 on CT.
2. Multiply the two results for each patient. The product is positive when both measurements are on the same side of their means (both above or both below), and negative when they are on opposite sides.
3. Average the products over all the patients (dividing by n − 1). That average is **r**. When high goes with high and low with low, most products are positive and r is close to +1. When there is no straight-line relationship, positive and negative products cancel out and r is close to 0.
4. The test asks whether r is further from 0 than chance would explain. It turns r into a [test statistic](../glossary.qmd#test-statistic){.term}, t = r × √(n − 2) ÷ √(1 − r²), and t into a [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" rebuilds r and t by hand.

### Look at the data first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

imaging <- read_csv("data/hip_preservation_imaging.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # one row per hip

ggplot(imaging, aes(torsion_ct_deg, torsion_budin_deg)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +   # see-through points show where they pile up
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +   # dashed line: the two methods read the same
  labs(x = "Femoral torsion on CT, degrees", y = "Femoral torsion on Budin view, degrees")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-association_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

imaging = pd.read_csv("data/hip_preservation_imaging.csv")   # one row per hip

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.scatter(imaging["torsion_ct_deg"], imaging["torsion_budin_deg"], alpha=0.6)   # see-through points show where they pile up
ax.axline((0, 0), slope=1, linestyle="--")   # dashed line: the two methods read the same
ax.set_xlabel("Femoral torsion on CT, degrees")
ax.set_ylabel("Femoral torsion on Budin view, degrees")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-association_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png)
:::
:::

:::

The points follow a straight line, with no extreme outliers, but a flatter one than the dashed line where the two methods would read the same: the Budin reading runs a little above CT at low torsion and below it at high torsion. (Torsion can be negative: the femur is then retroverted.)

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
torsion_corr <- cor.test(imaging$torsion_ct_deg, imaging$torsion_budin_deg)   # Pearson is the default
torsion_corr
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  imaging$torsion_ct_deg and imaging$torsion_budin_deg
t = 14.732, df = 78, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7861156 0.9065654
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.8576899 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
torsion_corr = stats.pearsonr(imaging["torsion_ct_deg"], imaging["torsion_budin_deg"])
print(torsion_corr)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
PearsonRResult(statistic=np.float64(0.8576898583915415), pvalue=np.float64(3.0576926692219362e-24))
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(torsion_corr.confidence_interval(confidence_level=0.95))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(0.786115630087847), high=np.float64(0.906565445098797))
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **cor** (R) or **statistic** (Python): Pearson's **r = 0.86**. It runs from −1 (a perfect falling line) through 0 (no straight-line relationship) to +1 (a perfect rising line).
- **t = 14.7, df = 78:** the test statistic and its degrees of freedom: 80 hips minus 2. Python doesn't print it.
- **p < 0.001** (R prints `p-value < 2.2e-16`, the smallest value it shows; Python prints `3.0576926692219362e-24`. Both are [scientific notation](../glossary.qmd#scientific-notation){.term} for numbers far below 0.001): a correlation this strong would be very unlikely if torsion on CT and on the Budin view were unrelated.
- **95% CI 0.79 to 0.91.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Under the hood: r and t by hand

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ct_sd_units <- (imaging$torsion_ct_deg - mean(imaging$torsion_ct_deg)) / sd(imaging$torsion_ct_deg)               # step 1: each CT value, in standard deviations from its mean
budin_sd_units <- (imaging$torsion_budin_deg - mean(imaging$torsion_budin_deg)) / sd(imaging$torsion_budin_deg)   # ... and each Budin value
r_by_hand <- sum(ct_sd_units * budin_sd_units) / (80 - 1)    # steps 2 and 3: multiply, add up, divide by n − 1 (80 hips)
r_by_hand
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.8576899
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
r_by_hand * sqrt(80 - 2) / sqrt(1 - r_by_hand^2)             # step 4: t
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 14.73238
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

ct_sd_units = (imaging["torsion_ct_deg"] - imaging["torsion_ct_deg"].mean()) / imaging["torsion_ct_deg"].std()               # step 1: each CT value, in standard deviations from its mean
budin_sd_units = (imaging["torsion_budin_deg"] - imaging["torsion_budin_deg"].mean()) / imaging["torsion_budin_deg"].std()   # ... and each Budin value
r_by_hand = (ct_sd_units * budin_sd_units).sum() / (80 - 1)   # steps 2 and 3: multiply, add up, divide by n − 1 (80 hips)
print(r_by_hand)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.8576898583915415
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(r_by_hand * np.sqrt(80 - 2) / np.sqrt(1 - r_by_hand ** 2))   # step 4: t
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
14.732384525508117
```


:::
:::

:::

The by-hand r is 0.86 and the by-hand t is 14.7: the `cor` and `t` in R's output. Python prints r as `statistic` and doesn't print t.
:::





### Effect size and 95% CI

**r is the effect size**: r = 0.86 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.91). As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium and 0.5 large. Squaring it gives the share of the variation in Budin torsion that goes with CT torsion: r² = 0.74, about three-quarters.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** The association between femoral torsion on CT and on the modified Budin view was measured with Pearson's correlation coefficient (r).
>
> **Results:** The correlation between femoral torsion on CT and on the modified Budin view was r = 0.86 (Pearson; 95% CI 0.79 to 0.91; p < 0.001; n = 80 hips).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: r only sees straight lines, isn't cause, and isn't agreement
A relationship that rises and then falls can have r close to 0, and one outlier can create or hide a correlation, so always look at the scatter plot first. And a correlation doesn't say which causes which, or whether something else (age, sex) drives both. To adjust for other variables, use [multiple regression](12-predict-from-several.qmd#multiple-linear-regression).

**A high r isn't agreement.** Two methods can rise and fall together and still read different angles. Here r = 0.86, yet the Budin reading was up to 12.9° away from CT, and 95% of the differences would be expected from −10.2° to 7.8° (the mean difference ± 1.96 standard deviations). Even those limits hide a trend: in the 8 hips with 25° or more on CT, the Budin reading averaged 7.0° lower. The code below computes these numbers. To ask whether one method can replace the other, use [Bland-Altman limits](../beyond/17-agreement.qmd#bland-altman).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
difference <- imaging$torsion_budin_deg - imaging$torsion_ct_deg   # Budin minus CT, one value per hip
max(abs(difference))                                  # the largest gap between the two methods
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12.9
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(difference) + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sd(difference)    # where 95% of the differences are expected
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -10.193064   7.810564
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
high_ct <- imaging$torsion_ct_deg >= 25               # hips with 25° or more on CT
sum(high_ct)                                          # how many
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 8
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(difference[high_ct])                             # their mean difference
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -6.9875
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}

print(difference.abs().max())                         # the largest gap between the two methods
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```


```
-10.193064369997792 7.810564369997792
```

```{.python .cell-code}
print(high_ct.sum(), difference[high_ct].mean())      # how many, and their mean difference
```

## Spearman correlation {#spearman}

**The question:** Are patients whose HOOS JR or KOOS JR improved more from before surgery to 1 year also more satisfied?

### When to use it

- Two variables on the same patients, at least one of them **ordinal** (satisfaction from 1 to 5), **[skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term}**, or with **outliers**.
- The relationship goes one way (always up, or always down) but needn't be a straight line. Spearman's ρ (rho) is Pearson's r calculated on the **ranks**.
- If both are roughly normal and the relationship is a straight line → [Pearson correlation](#pearson).

### What the test really does

Spearman's ρ is Pearson's r with one change: it is calculated on [ranks](../glossary.qmd#rank){.term} instead of the values themselves.

1. Rank the patients on the first variable, from lowest to highest. Tied values share the average of their ranks.
2. Do the same, separately, for the second variable.
3. Calculate [Pearson's r](#pearson) between the two sets of ranks. The result is **ρ**: close to +1 when patients who rank high on one variable also rank high on the other, close to −1 when the two rankings run in opposite directions, and close to 0 when they have nothing to do with each other.
4. The test asks whether ρ is further from 0 than chance would explain, and gives a [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

Because only the order counts, one outlier can't dominate the result, and a relationship that rises along a curve can still give a ρ close to 1. Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" rebuilds ρ by hand.

### Look at the data first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

change <- proms |>
  filter(visit %in% c("preop", "1yr")) |>
  select(case_id, visit, prom_score) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = prom_score) |>   # one row per case: preop and 1yr side by side
  mutate(improvement = `1yr` - preop) |>
  inner_join(select(cohort, case_id, satisfaction_1yr), by = "case_id") |>
  filter(!is.na(improvement), !is.na(satisfaction_1yr))          # both answers needed

nrow(change)   # procedures with both scores and a satisfaction answer
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 404
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(change, aes(factor(satisfaction_1yr), improvement)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Satisfaction at 1 year (1 = very dissatisfied, 5 = very satisfied)", y = "Improvement, points")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-association_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
  group_by(satisfaction_1yr) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_improvement = median(improvement))
```

## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")

wide = proms[proms["visit"].isin(["preop", "1yr"])].pivot(index="case_id", columns="visit", values="prom_score")
wide["improvement"] = wide["1yr"] - wide["preop"]   # one row per case: preop and 1yr side by side
change = wide.join(cohort.set_index("case_id")["satisfaction_1yr"]).dropna(subset=["improvement", "satisfaction_1yr"])

print(len(change))   # procedures with both scores and a satisfaction answer
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
404
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
levels = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
parts = ax.boxplot([change.loc[change["satisfaction_1yr"] == level, "improvement"] for level in levels], tick_labels=levels)
ax.set_xlabel("Satisfaction at 1 year (1 = very dissatisfied, 5 = very satisfied)")
ax.set_ylabel("Improvement, points")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-association_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png)
:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(change.groupby("satisfaction_1yr")["improvement"].agg(["count", "median"]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

satisfaction_1yr               
1.0                  14   25.35
2.0                  18   29.10
3.0                  43   33.80
4.0                 131   35.00
5.0                 198   43.75
```

404 procedures have both a pre-op and a 1-year score and a satisfaction answer (the first number printed). The median improvement climbs with each satisfaction level, from 25.4 points among the 14 very dissatisfied to 43.8 among the 198 very satisfied. Satisfaction has only five values, so there are many ties.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
satisfaction_corr <- cor.test(change$improvement, change$satisfaction_1yr,
                              method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)   # ties: no exact p-value
satisfaction_corr
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  change$improvement and change$satisfaction_1yr
S = 6764534, p-value = 1.111e-15
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.3844721 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
satisfaction_corr = stats.spearmanr(change["improvement"], change["satisfaction_1yr"])
print(satisfaction_corr)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
SignificanceResult(statistic=np.float64(0.3844721170232049), pvalue=np.float64(1.1107631277074974e-15))
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **rho** (R) or **statistic** (Python): **ρ = 0.38**. Like r, it runs from −1 to +1; here it says patients with larger improvements tend to give higher satisfaction scores.
- **S = 6764534** (R only): the test statistic, built from the differences between the two rankings. You don't need to report it.
- **p < 0.001** (R prints `1.111e-15` and Python the same number with more digits; this is [scientific notation](../glossary.qmd#scientific-notation){.term}: `e-15` means the decimal point moves 15 places to the left): a correlation this strong would be very unlikely if improvement and satisfaction were unrelated.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

```{.python .cell-code}
satisfaction_ranks = change["satisfaction_1yr"].rank()      # step 2: rank the satisfaction answers
```

Satisfaction has only five values, so its ranks are heavily tied: the 14 very dissatisfied share ranks 1 to 14 and each gets their average, 7.5; the 198 very satisfied each get 305.5. Pearson's r between the two sets of ranks is 0.38, the ρ both programs printed.
:::





### Effect size and 95% CI

**ρ is the effect size.** Neither `cor.test()` nor scipy gives its 95% CI, so R uses DescTools and Python uses the formula behind it (Fisher's z transformation).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
DescTools::SpearmanRho(change$improvement, change$satisfaction_1yr, conf.level = 0.95)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      rho    lwr.ci    upr.ci 
0.3844721 0.2980891 0.4646088 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
rho, n = satisfaction_corr.statistic, len(change)
z = np.arctanh(rho)                                 # Fisher's z: makes the CI symmetric
half_width = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) / np.sqrt(n - 3)
print(rho, np.tanh(z - half_width), np.tanh(z + half_width))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.3844721170232049 0.29808911349981776 0.4646088227466071
```


:::
:::

:::





ρ = 0.38 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.46): a moderate association, using the same rough guide as for r.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** The association between improvement in HOOS JR or KOOS JR from before surgery to 1 year and satisfaction at 1 year was measured with Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ).
>
> **Results:** Among 404 procedures with both scores and a satisfaction answer, the correlation between the change in HOOS JR or KOOS JR and satisfaction was ρ = 0.38 (Spearman; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.46; p < 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: two instruments in one number
Hip patients answer HOOS JR and knee patients KOOS JR. Both run from 0 to 100, but a point on one isn't guaranteed to mean the same as a point on the other. Pooling them is fine for a first look; in a paper, analyze hips and knees separately or say why you pooled them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: ties and the CI
- With fewer than 1290 patients, R's `cor.test()` tries an **exact** p-value. With ties it can't compute one, so it warns and falls back to the usual approximation, the one scipy always uses. `exact = FALSE` asks for the approximation directly, without the warning.
- Neither gives a CI for ρ. DescTools' `SpearmanRho()` and the Python formula use the same method: Fisher's z with a standard error of 1/√(n − 3).
:::

## Contingency coefficients {#contingency-coefficients}

**The question:** How strongly is ASA class linked with hypertension?

### When to use it

- Two **categorical** variables on the same patients. The chi-square test ([page 8](08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#chi-square)) asks whether they're linked at all; a contingency coefficient says **how strongly**.
- **Phi (φ)** is for 2 × 2 tables. **Cramér's V** works for any table size and equals φ (without its sign) on a 2 × 2 table. Both run from 0 (no link) to 1 (each category of one predicts the other exactly).
- **Pearson's contingency coefficient (C)** is older. Its maximum is below 1 and depends on the table's size (it is √((k − 1) ÷ k), where k is the smaller of the number of rows and the number of columns: √(1 ÷ 2) = 0.71 for a table with two columns), which makes it hard to read, so prefer V.
- The chi-square p-value needs every [expected count](../glossary.qmd#expected-count){.term} to be at least 5.

### What the test really does

A contingency coefficient turns the chi-square statistic into a number between 0 and 1 that says how strong the link is.

1. Run the [chi-square test](08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#chi-square). It compares the table you observed with the table you'd expect if the two variables were unrelated, and sums up the gap between them as χ².
2. χ² grows with the strength of the link, but also with the number of patients: double every count in the table and χ² doubles, although the link is no stronger.
3. **Cramér's V** takes the sample size out: V = √(χ² ÷ (n × (k − 1))), where n is the number of patients and k is the smaller of the number of rows and the number of columns.
4. **Pearson's C** uses a slightly different formula, C = √(χ² ÷ (χ² + n)), which can never reach 1.

Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" works out V and C by hand.

### Read the output

- **X-squared = 23.18:** the chi-square statistic. **df = 3:** (4 ASA classes − 1) × (2 columns − 1).
- **p < 0.001** (R prints `3.702e-05`, [scientific notation](../glossary.qmd#scientific-notation){.term} for 0.000037; it is the third number on Python's first line): a link this strong would be very unlikely if hypertension were equally common in every ASA class.
- **Expected counts:** what each cell would hold if ASA class and hypertension were unrelated. The smallest is 7.83, in the last row, first column (ASA 4 without hypertension): 18 procedures in ASA 4 × 261 without hypertension ÷ 600. Every expected count is at least 5, so the p-value is reliable.

## 🔍 Under the hood: V and C by hand

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
chi_square <- unname(asa_test$statistic)
n_procedures <- sum(asa_hypertension)                # all 600 procedures
sqrt(chi_square / (n_procedures * (2 - 1)))          # Cramér's V: the smaller of 4 rows and 2 columns is 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.1965592
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sqrt(chi_square / (chi_square + n_procedures))       # Pearson's C
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.1928687
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
doubled <- unname(chisq.test(2 * asa_hypertension)$statistic)
c(doubled, sqrt(doubled / (2 * n_procedures)))       # step 2: with every count doubled, chi-square doubles and V stays the same
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 46.3626066  0.1965592
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

chi_square = asa_test.statistic
n_procedures = asa_hypertension.to_numpy().sum()                # all 600 procedures
print(np.sqrt(chi_square / (n_procedures * (2 - 1))))           # Cramér's V: the smaller of 4 rows and 2 columns is 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.19655916548428345
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(np.sqrt(chi_square / (chi_square + n_procedures)))        # Pearson's C
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.19286868402903107
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
doubled = stats.chi2_contingency(2 * asa_hypertension).statistic
print(doubled, np.sqrt(doubled / (2 * n_procedures)))           # step 2: with every count doubled, chi-square doubles and V stays the same
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
46.36260664305351 0.19655916548428345
```


:::
:::

:::

V = √(23.18 ÷ 600) = 0.20 and C = √(23.18 ÷ (23.18 + 600)) = 0.19, the numbers the functions in the next step print. Doubling every count doubles χ² to 46.36 but leaves V at 0.20: V measures the strength of the link, not the size of the study.
:::

```
Cramer's V |       95% CI
-------------------------
0.20       | [0.12, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}

```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Cramer's V (adj.) |       95% CI
--------------------------------
0.18              | [0.10, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}

```

```
Pearson's C |       95% CI
--------------------------

```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print(stats.contingency.association(asa_hypertension, method="cramer"))    # Cramér's V
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.19655916548428345
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(stats.contingency.association(asa_hypertension, method="pearson"))   # Pearson's C
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.19286868402903107
```


:::
:::

:::





**Cramér's V = 0.20**, a small-to-medium association (as a rough guide for tables with two rows or columns, 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium and 0.5 large). R also prints a one-sided 95% CI (0.12 to 1.00): V can't be negative, so only its lower bound is informative. scipy doesn't compute this CI. R's second result, headed `Cramer's V (adj.)`, is explained in the R vs Python box. Pearson's C is 0.19 here, but its ceiling for this table is 0.71, not 1, so the same number means more than it seems: one more reason to report V.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** The association between ASA class and hypertension was tested with the chi-square test, with Cramér's V as the effect size.
>
> **Results:** Hypertension was present in 12 of 36 procedures (33.3%) in ASA 1 and 16 of 18 (88.9%) in ASA 4 (χ² = 23.2, df = 3, p < 0.001; Cramér's V = 0.20, one-sided 95% CI 0.12 to 1.00).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: V gives the strength, not the pattern
Shuffling the rows of the table doesn't change V, so V can't say that hypertension rises **steadily** with ASA class. The row percentages show the pattern; put them in your Results. If the categories are ordered and you expect a trend, a test for trend can be more powerful than the plain chi-square test.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: Cramér's V has two versions
effectsize's `cramers_v()` and `phi()` apply a small-sample bias correction by default (here V = 0.18, the result headed `Cramer's V (adj.)` in the R tab), while scipy's `association()` doesn't. `adjust = FALSE` turns it off so the two match; whichever you use, say which in your Methods. On a 2 × 2 table, `association(method="cramer")` gives φ without its sign.
:::

```{.python .cell-code}
alpha_corr = stats.pearsonr(imaging["alpha_dunn45_deg"], imaging["alpha_frogleg_deg"])

```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

**2.** A colleague asks whether older patients stay in hospital longer. Which correlation would you use, and what do you find?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Length of stay is strongly right-skewed with many ties ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#transform)): **Spearman correlation**.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cor.test(cohort$los_days, cohort$age, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  cohort$los_days and cohort$age
S = 30777868, p-value = 0.0003644
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.1450568 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
DescTools::SpearmanRho(cohort$los_days, cohort$age, conf.level = 0.95)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       rho     lwr.ci     upr.ci 
0.14505684 0.06577619 0.22251757 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
los_corr = stats.spearmanr(cohort["los_days"], cohort["age"])
z, half_width = np.arctanh(los_corr.statistic), stats.norm.ppf(0.975) / np.sqrt(len(cohort) - 3)
print(los_corr, np.tanh(z - half_width), np.tanh(z + half_width))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
SignificanceResult(statistic=np.float64(0.14505684292632762), pvalue=np.float64(0.0003643931688756085)) 0.0657761944392072 0.22251756976389372
```


:::
:::

:::

> **Results:** The correlation between age and length of stay was ρ = 0.15 (Spearman; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.22; p < 0.001).

Older patients tended to stay slightly longer, but the association is weak.
:::
